questions.q: Why must you confirm SSH key-based login works BEFORE disabling password authentication in sshd_config?
options: Disabling passwords automatically enables key-based login
sshd requires password authentication to be disabled first for keys to work
If key-based login isn't already working and you disable passwords, you can lock yourself out of the server permanently
It makes no difference which order you do it in
questions.explain: If the key-based login hasn't been verified first and password auth is then disabled, there is no remaining way to log in — a classic self-lockout.

questions.q: Why confirm your non-root user can `sudo` before disabling root login over SSH?
options: Root login must stay enabled forever for safety
sudo access is unrelated to root login
Once root login is disabled, your sudo-capable account becomes the only path to perform admin tasks, so it must already work
sudo only works while root login is still enabled
questions.explain: With root login disabled, all administration happens through a regular account using sudo. If that account's sudo access isn't confirmed first, there's no way left to perform privileged tasks.

questions.q: Why allow SSH through the firewall BEFORE enabling a default-deny firewall policy?
options: SSH traffic is always allowed regardless of firewall rules
Firewalls can't have any rules before being enabled
It doesn't matter — the order has no effect
A default-deny firewall blocks all traffic, including SSH, the moment it's enabled — without an SSH allow rule already in place, you lose your own connection
questions.explain: Enabling a default-deny firewall with no exception for SSH immediately cuts off the very connection being used to configure the server.

questions.q: According to the capstone plan, what confirms the systemd service piece is 'done'?
options: `systemctl status` (or `systemctl is-active`) shows the internal tool running as a managed, enabled service
The service's code compiles without errors
The tool was started manually and is currently running in a terminal session
The service process appears in `ps aux` at least once
questions.explain: The brief specifies the internal tool should run as a systemd unit, enabled to start on boot and confirmed running via systemctl — not a manually started process.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the final 'log review' step in the capstone checklist?
options: It's optional and mainly for documentation purposes
To confirm, from the logs themselves, that the login path, the service, and the cron job are actually behaving the way they were configured
To delete old logs and free disk space
To generate a performance benchmark report
questions.explain: The brief frames log review as verification — checking journalctl and auth logs to confirm key-based logins are succeeding, root login attempts aren't appearing, and scheduled jobs ran as expected.
